items.title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls \ Anthropic
items.summary:
Deferral of this kind is hard to detect. Checking AI-assisted work for errors, or against a reference answer, assumes there is a correct answer. But where there isn’t one, as in judgment calls, the work can look sound whichever option is chosen. Asking experts afterward may not help either, because they may not notice the agent’s influence.

This isn’t an argument for using AI less. Used well, AI could expand people’s agency rather than eroding it. We suggest three areas for future study: [...] Changing institutions. Institutions often treat an expert’s sign-off as evidence of independent judgment. As AI does more of the work, that assumption becomes shakier. Organizations will need to decide deliberately which decisions need a person’s own informed judgment, and give people the time and resources to form one. Judgment also depends on skill, and people who stop making these decisions may lose the ability to make them. As models become more capable, institutions will need an explicit [...] The same problem applies to AI safety research. Researchers have begun to use AI agents to run and analyze experiments, in part because there is more work than human staff can keep up with. Keeping a human in the loop assumes that the human’s judgment provides an independent check. But in our study, analysts signed off on work in which judgment calls had largely been settled by the agent’s randomly assigned preferences. items.title: Inside Democrats’ 2028 brainstorm on AI safety - POLITICO
items.summary: The two-day event held just days after the midterm election underscores how 2028 hopefuls are viewing AI as a crucial part of their potential presidential bids after voter discontent over issues like AI data centers played a role in Democrats’ sweeping wins last week. [...] The meeting featured one-on-one interviews and group discussions of what the party should actually do about AI, according to three people with direct knowledge of the event, granted anonymity to candidly discuss private conversations. The people said reports from AI safety researchers scared many of the more traditional Democrats in attendance. [...] The event, hosted by Who Decides — an AI safety advocacy organization run by New York Assemblymember Alex Bores and his former legislative aide Anna Myers — also cemented the organization as an early Democratic power player in the AI and politics fight. Bores has become a key voice on AI safety since authoring a landmark law in the state and losing a congressional primary amid intense opposition spending from the industry.
